title: When Quitting Is Harder Than Joining: The Behavioural Economics of Subscription Cancellation
author: Qinlei Wang
abstract: Subscription retention is often treated as evidence of consumer loyalty, but continued payment can reflect genuine preference, inattention, delayed action, switching costs, or deliberately burdensome cancellation design. This literature review examines how behavioural economics and choice architecture complicate what retention actually tells us about consumer preference.

title: Is Sexual Violence Without Killing Sufficient to Constitute Genocide?
author: Adam Salim
abstract: This article examines whether systematic sexual violence can constitute genocide even in the absence of mass killing. Focusing on the Foča campaign during the Bosnian War, it considers international criminal law, genocidal intent, institutional coordination, forced reproduction, and Claudia Card's concept of social death to explore where the conceptual and legal boundaries of genocide should be drawn.

title: After Loss, the Self Relearns to Belong: A Psychological Reading of Zucchini in My Life as a Zucchini
author: Apurba Roy and Samiur Prapon
university: Pundra University of Science & Technology; North South University, Bangladesh
abstract: The article looks at Zucchini’s psychological development in Claude Barras’s book My Life as a Zucchini (2016), concentrating on the way in which grief, disruption of attachment, the need for peer belonging, coping mechanisms, self-efficacy, and resilience interact in the process of rebuilding a child’s sense of self. Instead of analysing Zucchini’s behaviour using a diagnostic approach, the study makes use of Piaget’s cognitive-developmental theory, Erikson’s psychosocial theory, Bowlby’s attachment theory, Bandura’s social learning and self-efficacy theories, Lazarus and Folkman’s theory of coping, Masten’s idea of resilience, and Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory. By looking at particular scenes it shows how Zucchini progresses from feelings of fear, guilt and relational insecurity to a state of agency, emotional integration and a sense of belonging. The article maintains that his development should not be seen as the disappearance of grief but rather as a gradual reorganisation of his relational world, and that it is because of reliable care from his caregivers, peer recognition and opportunities for meaningful action that he is able to turn adversity into a renewed ability to trust and attach.

title: Climate Justice after Institutional Failure
author: James Machado
abstract: An examination of climate responsibility, Indigenous collective continuance, institutional failure, and what climate justice can require when the institutions responsible for environmental harm repeatedly fail to act.

title: Ecofeminism, Social Ecology, and Bioregionalism
author: James Machado
abstract: James Machado examines ecofeminism, social ecology, and bioregionalism, arguing that ecological crises are inseparable from social hierarchies and systems of domination.

title: Bridging the Gap: Addressing Health Disparities in Punjabi Communities Through Culturally Responsive Health Education
author: Jasmine Kaur, Mansa Kaur, and Japji Kaur
abstract: Jasmine Kaur, Mansa Kaur, and Japji Kaur of Sehat e Punjab examine health disparities in Punjabi communities and how culturally responsive health education, health literacy, and community outreach can improve preventive care and health equity.

title: Emotions as a Teacher: Remembering Rhymes for Young Ghouls
author: James Machado
abstract: James Machado examines how Jeff Barnaby's Rhymes for Young Ghouls uses color, sound, perspective, pacing, and visual technique to make viewers experience the emotional weight of oppression.

title: The Irrevocability of Culture
author: James Machado
abstract: James Machado examines how Sydney Freeland's Rez Ball portrays Navajo culture, basketball, resilience, grief, and community as inseparable from the meaning of winning.

title: Stress and Student Performance in Higher Education
author: Jacob Gannon
abstract: Jacob Gannon reviews evidence on how persistent and acute stress affect academic performance in higher education, examining assessment design, coping resources, and the structural conditions that shape student stress.

title: Georgia O’Keeffe: Beauty and Symbolism of the Interwar Period
author: Georgia Lewis
university: School of the Art Institute of Chicago
abstract: Georgia Lewis examines Georgia O’Keeffe’s floral, urban, and landscape works as expressions of beauty, symbolism, and artistic independence across and beyond the interwar period.

title: The Uniform Effect
author: Sanya Khan
preview: Sanya Khan traces the paradox of uniforms through psychology, culture, and fashion, asking what uniforms grant us, what they cost us, and why we keep choosing them anyway.

title: The Ballerina Effect
author: Sanya Khan
abstract: Sanya Khan traces the ballerina from European court culture through balletcore, examining how fashion, biomechanics, racial exclusion, and the aestheticization of discipline converge in the enduring image of the ballerina.

title: Can Major Earthquakes Be Predicted? Lessons from the 2011 Japan Earthquake
author: Karthikeya Nandi
abstract: Karthikeya Nandi evaluates the reliability of foreshocks, changes in seismic velocity, seismic gaps, and surface deformation as predictive indicators of major earthquakes, using the 2011 Japan earthquake as a case study.

title: Balancing Climate Policy with Economic Interests
author: Braydon Perko
abstract: Braydon Perko argues that delaying U.S. climate action now carries far greater long-term economic costs than investing in renewable energy and climate resilience.

title: The Alien Invasion Has Already Happened: An Introduction to Afrofuturism
author: Georgia Lewis
university: School of the Art Institute of Chicago
abstract: Georgia Lewis introduces Afrofuturism through film, music, and art, arguing that for Black people the alien invasion of colonialism has already happened—and that Afrofuturist artists reclaim that narrative to imagine worlds of liberation.

title: Capturing Wonder: Jacques-Henri Lartigue and the Art of Vernacular Photography
author: Georgia Lewis
university: School of the Art Institute of Chicago
abstract: Georgia Lewis examines Jacques-Henri Lartigue's vernacular photography through three qualities: his childlike genuineness, his economic standing and social class, and his fascination with the technological advancements of Belle Époque France.

title: Over-Reliance on AI and the Decline of Student Cognitive Skills
author: Karthikeya Nandi
abstract: This article examines how over-reliance on AI in education can weaken critical thinking and decision-making, and proposes school-level strategies to preserve cognitive skills while using AI responsibly.

title: Work, Meaning, and the Search for Fulfillment: A Philosophical Reading of ‘Office Space’
author: Braydon Perko
abstract: Braydon Perko examines Office Space through the philosophical frameworks of Graeber, Kant, and Mill, arguing that the dissatisfaction of Peter, Michael, and Samir reflects a broader failure of modern workplaces to provide the meaning, autonomy, and higher forms of satisfaction that genuine fulfillment requires.

title: The Moral Work of Anger
author: Braydon Perko
abstract: This article argues that anger can be a morally apt response to injustice and a catalyst for accountability, collective action, and social change.

title: The Body That Drives: Merleau-Ponty’s Phenomenology of Embodiment in Baby Driver
author: Harrison McLain
abstract: Harrison McLain examines Edgar Wright’s Baby Driver through Maurice Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenology of embodiment, arguing that the film enacts key claims about the body-schema, the intentional arc, and sedimented habit—making it one of the most philosophically precise films in recent cinema.

title: Beyond the Diss Track: A Sociological Analysis of Kendrick Lamar’s Not Like Us
author: Luke Marshall
abstract: This article examines Kendrick Lamar’s 2024 song Not Like Us through a sociological lens. By analyzing themes of social stratification, social mobility, race, ethnicity, cultural appropriation, and colonialism, the article explores how contemporary hip-hop can serve as a form of social commentary. Rather than focusing on the celebrity dispute itself, the analysis demonstrates how popular music reflects broader debates surrounding identity, authenticity, power, and cultural ownership.

title: Revenue Recognition in the Airline Industry: A Case Study of Delta Air Lines
author: Luke Marshall
abstract: This finance case study examines how Delta Air Lines applies ASC 606 to passenger ticket sales, its SkyMiles loyalty program, and ancillary services, and what those accounting choices mean for investors.

title: When Goodwill Disappears: Lessons from Coty's $3.9 Billion Impairment
author: Luke Marshall
abstract: This finance case study examines Coty Inc.'s 2019 goodwill impairment following its acquisition of Procter & Gamble's beauty brands.
